WHO Family of International Classifications (FIC)

The WHO Family of International Classifications and Terminologies includes:

  • the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD),
  • the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF),
  • and the International Classification of Health Interventions (ICHI). 

These Reference Classifications serve as the global standards for health data, for clinician documentation at the point of care, and for statistical aggregation.

Through the integration of terminology and classification in a single framework, WHO classifications provide the openly permitted, Member-State-accountable foundation on which interoperable health information systems and the next generation of clinical AI are built.

WHO-FIC Maintenance Platform

Benefits of WHO-FIC

ICD-11, ICF and ICHI are key for effective knowledge representation and interoperability.

WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) allows all healthcare workers (and patients) to communicate using one (technical) language.

WHO-FIC and their shared terminology provide the substrate on which clinical natural language processing and AI systems are built, openly permitted for use across all WHO Member States under WHO governance..

WHO-FIC with their shared terminology are key for effective text mining or text analytics (the process of deriving high-quality information from plain and unstructured text).

WHO-FIC classifications are governed through Member State processes, making them the open and Member-State-accountable foundation for equitable AI in health.

ICD-11, ICF, and ICHI: empowering better health with smarter use of resources.

Used by

  • Governments — to allocate resources
  • Researchers — to collaborate across borders
  • Doctors — to document their cases
  • Health providers — in algorithms for decision support
  • Hospitals — to count the frequency of health problems
  • Laboratories — to exchange investigative data
  • AI developers — for lawful training of clinical decision-support and language systems on terminology-encoded health data, open and permitted across all WHO Member States
  • Insurance companies — for billing purposes
  • National digital health authorities — as the governance foundation for interoperable health information systems.
  • International organizations — to assess trends in public health

Reference Classifications

 

International Statistical Classification of Diseases and related health problems: 
Diagnoses, injuries, findings, primary care...

 


International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health:
Describes functional health status and social impact (bio-psycho-social model)...

 


Interventions for treatment, prevention and diagnostics: Medical, nursing, rehabilitation, laboratory, imaging, ultrasound, public health...

    Common Foundation - Terminology components

    The Foundation Component represents the entire WHO-FIC universe. It is a multidimensional collection of interconnected entities and synonyms. These entities consist of diseases, disorders, injuries, external causes, signs and symptoms, functional descriptions, interventions, and extension codes. ICD-11 statistical core (MMS) is derived from this foundation, ICF and ICHI will follow. Currently, with over hundred thousand entities and the ontological design of the foundation component, more than one million terms can be captured. The Foundation Component is the openly governed, Member-State-accountable knowledge base for the encoding of health data globally, permitted for use across all WHO Member States.

    The Foundation Component also includes WHO terminologies such as: 

    • WHO INN (non proprietary names - medicaments)/ATC
    • WHO Devices
    • Histopathology (tumours)
    • Anatomy
    • Details of external causes
    • Severity
    • Infectious agents
    • Sites and activities
    • Rare diseases

    Derived classifications

    Derived classifications are extensions of reference classifications, and are created for use within a specialty setting and are derived from the common foundation.

    • See all derived classifications  

    Related classifications

    Related classifications are complementary to reference and derived classifications, and cover specialty areas not otherwise described in the Family of International Classifications (FIC). 

    • See all related classifications

                    <h1 class="dynamic-content__title-text">HIV</h1>
            </div>
        </header>

        
        <section class="dynamic-content__section dynamic-content__container">
            <div class="row">
                <div class="col-md-7">
                    <div class="dynamic-content__section-content">
                        
                        <div class="sf_cols tabWidget health-topic_tabWidget tabWrapper" style="display: block;">
                            <div class="sf_colsOut flex-clear" data-placeholder-label="Tab wrapper">
                                <div class="ul-tabs--wrapper">
                                    <ul class="tabs"><li id="tab_1" class="tabs__item active shown" style="width: 33.3333%;"><a href="#tab=tab_1"><span>Overview</span></a></li><li id="tab_2" class="tabs__item shown" style="width: 33.3333%;"><a href="#tab=tab_2"><span>Symptoms</span></a></li><li id="tab_3" class="tabs__item shown" style="width: 33.3333%;"><a href="#tab=tab_3"><span>Treatment</span></a></li><li class="mobile-tab tabs__item hidden" style="width: 33.3333%;"><a href="#tab="><span>More</span></a></li></ul>
                                </div>
                                <div class="sf_colsIn single-tabContent">
        <div class="sf_cols singleTabWrapper visible" data-id="tab_1">
            <div class="sf_colsOut tabHeaderWrapper" data-sf-element="Tab header" data-placeholder-label="Tab header">
                <div class="sf_colsIn tabHeaderText">
                    <div class="sf-content-block content-block">
                        Overview
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="sf_colsOut tabContent" data-sf-element="Tab contents" data-placeholder-label="Tab contents">
                <div class="sf_colsIn">
                    <p>Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is an infection that attacks the body’s immune system, specifically the white blood cells called CD4 cells. HIV destroys these CD4 cells, weakening a person’s immunity against opportunistic infections, such
    as tuberculosis and fungal infections, severe bacterial infections and some cancers.</p><p>WHO recommends that every person who may be at risk of HIV should access testing. <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/populations">People at increased risk of acquiring HIV</a> should seek comprehensive and effective HIV prevention, testing and treatment services. <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/testing-diagnostics">HIV infection can be diagnosed </a>using simple and affordable rapid diagnostic tests, as well as self-tests. It is important that <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/testing-diagnostics/hiv-testing-services">HIV testing services</a> follow the 5Cs: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection with treatment and
    other services. </p><p>People diagnosed with HIV should be offered and linked to <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment">antiretroviral treatment (ART) </a>as
 soon as possible following diagnosis and <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/strategic-information/person-centered-hiv-patient-monitoring">periodically monitored</a> using clinical and laboratory parameters, including the test to measure virus in the blood (viral load). If ART is taken consistently, this treatment also <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/prevention">prevents HIV transmission </a>to others.</p><p>At diagnosis or soon after starting ART, a CD4 cell count should be checked to assess a person’s immune status. The CD4 cell count is a blood test used to assess progression of HIV disease, including risk for developing <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/chronic-comorbidities-and-coinfections">opportunistic infections</a> and guides the use of preventive treatment. The normal range of CD4 count is from 500 to 1500 cells/mm3
    of blood, and it progressively decreases over time in persons who are not receiving or not responding well to ART. If the person’s CD4 cell count falls below 200, their immunity is severely compromised, leaving them susceptible to infections
    and death. Someone with a CD4 count below 200 is described as having an <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/advanced-hiv-disease">advanced HIV disease (AHD)</a>.</p><p>HIV viral load measures the amount of virus in the blood. This test is used to monitor the level of viral replication and effectiveness of ART. The treatment goal is to reduce the viral load in the blood to undetectable levels (less than 50 copies/ml),
    and the persistent presence of detectable viral load (greater than 1000 copies/ml) in people living with HIV on ART is an indicator of inadequate treatment response and the need to change or adjust the treatment regimen. </p><p>WHO’s 2022–2030 <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/strategies/global-health-sector-strategies">global health sector strategy on HIV</a> aims
 to reduce HIV infections from 1.5 million in 2020 to 335 000 by 2030, and deaths from 680 000 in 2020 to under 240 000 in 2030.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sf_cols singleTabWrapper" data-id="tab_2">
            <div class="sf_colsOut tabHeaderWrapper" data-sf-element="Tab header" data-placeholder-label="Tab header">
                <div class="sf_colsIn tabHeaderText">
                    <div class="sf-content-block content-block">
                        Symptoms
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="sf_colsOut tabContent" data-sf-element="Tab contents" data-placeholder-label="Tab contents">
                <div class="sf_colsIn">
                    <p>Many people do not feel symptoms of HIV in the first few months after infection and may not know that they are infected. Others may experience influenza-like symptoms, including fever, headache, rash and sore throat. However, these first few months are when the virus is most infectious.</p><p>As the disease progresses, symptoms will be expanded and more pronounced. These can include swollen lymph nodes, weight loss, fever, diarrhoea and cough. HIV weakens the body’s ability to fight other infections, and without treatment people will become more susceptible to <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/chronic-comorbidities-and-coinfections">other severe illnesses</a> such as <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/tuberculosis-hiv">tuberculosis</a>, cryptococcal meningitis, bacterial infections and some cancers including lymphomas and Kaposi’s sarcoma.</p><p><a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/testing-diagnostics">Diagnosis of HIV </a>uses rapid tests that provide same-day results and can  be done at home, although a laboratory test is required to confirm the infection. This early identification greatly improves treatment options and reduces the risk of transmission to other people including sexual or drug-sharing partners.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sf_cols singleTabWrapper" data-id="tab_3">
            <div class="sf_colsOut tabHeaderWrapper" data-sf-element="Tab header" data-placeholder-label="Tab header">
                <div class="sf_colsIn tabHeaderText">
                    <div class="sf-content-block content-block">
                        Treatment
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="sf_colsOut tabContent" data-sf-element="Tab contents" data-placeholder-label="Tab contents">
                <div class="sf_colsIn">
                    <p>HIV is fully preventable. Effective <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment">antiretroviral treatment (ART) </a>prevents <a href="/initiatives/triple-elimination-initiative-of-mother-to-child-transmission-of-hiv-syphilis-and-hepatitis-b">HIV transmission from mother to child </a>during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding. Someone who is on antiretroviral therapy and virally suppressed will not pass HIV to their sexual partners.</p><p>Condoms prevent HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, and prophylaxis use antiretroviral medicines to prevent HIV. <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/prevention/voluntary-medical-male-circumcision">Male circumcision</a> is recommended in high-burden countries in eastern and southern Africa. Harm reduction (needle syringe programmes and opioid substitution therapy) prevents HIV and other blood-borne infections for <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/populations">people who inject drugs</a>.</p><p>HIV is treated with antiretroviral therapy consisting of one or more medicines. ART does not cure HIV but reduces its replication in the blood, thereby reducing the viral load to an undetectable level.</p><p>ART enables people living with HIV to lead healthy, productive lives. It also works as an effective prevention, <a href="/news/item/20-07-2018-viral-suppression-for-hiv-treatment-success-and-prevention-of-sexual-transmission-of-hiv">reducing the risk of onward transmission by 96%</a>.</p><p>ART should be taken every day throughout the person’s life. People can continue with <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/monitoring-toxicity-of-antiretrovirals">safe and effective ART</a> if they adhere to their treatment. In cases when ART becomes ineffective - <a href="/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/treatment/hiv-drug-resistance">HIV drug resistance</a> - due to reasons such as lost contact with health care providers and drug stockouts, people will need to switch to other medicines to protect their health.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

<div class="sf-content-block content-block">
    <div><p style="font-size:30px;text-align:left;line-height:35px;">Making WHO reliable, impactful, relevant in every country</p><p>WHO is committed to enhancing its effectiveness and making a meaningful impact in countries, ensuring that we can effectively serve our Member States. Our approach involves empowering country offices through a comprehensive bottom-up process, spearheaded by WHO representatives in collaboration with the Action for Results Group. Since the proposal of an Action Plan in February 2023, significant strides have been made to fortify country offices, ensuring they are equipped with the necessary resources, personnel, and streamlined operations. This strategic focus enables WHO to deliver tangible results where it matters most—at the country level.</p><p>The Action Plan for Country Office Strengthening” proposed by the Action for Results Group underpins <a href="/about/transformation">WHO's Transformation Agenda</a>, enhancing our capacity to respond effectively to diverse health challenges in the countries and increasing the impact on people’s health.</p><p> </p></div>
</div>

<div id="PageContent_C065_Col00" class="sf_colsIn background-widget" data-sf-element="Background widget" data-placeholder-label="Background widget"><div id="PageContent_C066_Col00" class="sf_colsIn container" data-sf-element="Container" data-placeholder-label="Container"><div class="row" data-sf-element="Row">

<div class="sf-content-block content-block">
    <div><h2>Action for Results Group</h2><hr><p>In January 2023, the Action for Results Group (ARG) was founded with a focused mission: to accelerate the empowerment of WHO country offices, aligning with the Organization's enduring commitment to meeting countries' needs effectively. The group, consisting of two WHO Representatives (WRs) from each of WHO's six regions, was carefully designed to ensure broad representation and informed decision-making. The ARG, with combined insights and expertise of all WRs, carefully created an Action Plan designed to initiate lasting transformations tailored to the unique requirements of each country.</p><p> </p></div>
</div>

    </div>
    <div id="PageContent_C106_Col01" class="sf_colsIn col-md-1 empty" data-sf-element="Column 2" data-placeholder-label="Column 2"></div>
    <div id="PageContent_C106_Col02" class="sf_colsIn col-md-5" data-sf-element="Column 3" data-placeholder-label="Column 3">

    <a href="https://cdn.who.int/media/images/default-source/who_homepage/action-for-results-group.jpg?sfvrsn=2516e062_4">
            <div class="sf-image thumb">
        <img class="lazy" data-src="https://cdn.who.int/media/images/default-source/who_homepage/action-for-results-group.tmb-1920v.jpg?sfvrsn=2516e062_2" data-image="https://cdn.who.int/media/images/default-source/who_homepage/action-for-results-group.tmb-1920v.jpg?sfvrsn=2516e062_2" title="Action for Results Group" alt="Group photo of WHO Director-General and the members of the Action for Results Group." src="https://cdn.who.int/media/images/default-source/who_homepage/action-for-results-group.tmb-479v.jpg?sfvrsn=2516e062_2">

<div class="row" data-sf-element="Row">
    <div id="PageContent_C049_Col00" class="sf_colsIn col-md-7" data-sf-element="Column 1" data-placeholder-label="Column 1">
<div class="section-heading">
            <h2>Strengthening WHO country offices for greater impact</h2>

</div>



<div class="sf-content-block content-block">
    <div><p>The Action Plan to strengthen WHO country offices addresses critical capacity needs, while ultimately striving to make WHO more reliable and impactful. A key component is its differentiated “core predictable country presence”, which recognises the need to build differentiated core capacities in all country offices, but varies them depending on the level of WHO support provided to countries based on their needs.</p><p>The Action Plan's key areas are as follows:</p><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>Enhanced delegation of authority to WRs in countries</h3><p>In 2023, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and five WHO regional directors issued a joint global delegation of authority to WHO Country Representatives, to enable them to provide more responsive and timely support to Member States. This significant step in decentralizing leadership recognizes the vital role of WHO Country Office heads and will empower them to take a stronger leadership role in the countries they serve.</p><p> </p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="1." data-open="1. Enhanced delegation of authority to WRs in countries" class="more-button-label"><text>1.</text><text>1. Enhanced delegation of authority to WRs in countries</text></div></span>
 </div></div><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>Core predictable WHO country presence, implemented and financed</h3><p>Recognizing the need to have core staff positions that are predictably financed in WHO country offices, the ARG recommended a model based on a minimum core structure and capacity for all country offices. This core predictable country presence (CPCP) will help ensure country offices are fit-for-purpose with the required technical and managerial capacities. Importantly, the CPCP is differentiated by country office “typology”, based on a rigorous process that looks at country context, situation and need. This also helps set the support provided – policy dialogue, strategic support, technical assistance or service delivery. The typology will be revised when critically needed based on the changing situation in countries.</p><p>→ <a href="https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/country-strategy-and-support/cpcp-differentiated-approach.pdf?sfvrsn=10a56379_3">Core predictable WHO country presence differentiated approach table</a></p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="2." data-open="2. Core predictable WHO country presence, implemented and financed" class="more-button-label"><text>2.</text> <text>2. Core predictable WHO country presence, implemented and financed</text></div></span>
 </div></div><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>A more mobile workforce to better support countries</h3><p>An ARG-supported new global staff mobility programme is underway to help put the right workforce in the right place at the right time. It will respond effectively to a changing environment, enhance professional development and introduce culture change and promote “one WHO”. The programme will be geared to the needs of countries, so as to strengthen health systems and services to benefit people in countries.</p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="3." data-open="3. A more mobile workforce to better support countries" class="more-button-label"><text>3.</text> <text>3. A more mobile workforce to better support countries</text></div></span>
 </div></div><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>Streamlined planning of country level work</h3><p>Planning of country-level work is being sharpened so it is focused on better alignment with national health priorities, and results delivery. Investments in human and financial resources in the country offices will not only be geared towards delivering on these priorities, but strengthen country-level work planning, capacity building and implementation to address health issues which require cross-sector collaborations. The entire results-based management approach will also be streamlined to minimize the process burden for country offices and to drive impact in countries.</p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="4." data-open="4. Streamlined planning of country level work" class="more-button-label"><text>4.</text> <text>4. Streamlined planning of country level work</text></div></span>
 </div></div><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>Improved human resources management</h3><p>The ARG has proposed a comprehensive set of actions to ensure human resources management is more efficient and geared towards harnessing staff capacities and talents. These include making the recruitment and selection process faster and more transparent. It will be geared towards placing the right people in the most demanding places at the right time.</p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="5." data-open="5. Improved human resources management" class="more-button-label"><text>5.</text> <text>5. Improved human resources management</text></div></span>
 </div></div><div class="more-content-wrapper"><div data-class="more-content" class="more-content"><div data-class="more-content-inner" class="more-content-inner"><h3>More open communication between staff across the Organization</h3><p>A new internal WHO policy aims to facilitate a free exchange of ideas and information among all staff members, no matter their grade, office or level of the Organization. This pursues the goal of the WHO transformation agenda for a more modern, seamless, impacted-focused Organization better equipped to support countries. It aligns with the ARG’s Action Plan to bring together all capacities at all levels to support Member States as one Organization.</p><p> </p></div></div><div data-class="more-button" class="more-button"><span style="font-weight:bold;"><div data-class="more-button-label" data-close="6." data-open="6. More open communication between staff across the Organization" class="more-button-label"><text>6.</text> <text>6. More open communication between staff across the Organization</text></div></span>
 </div></div><p> </p><p>In just a few months, the plan has catalyzed significant changes with profound implications for countries worldwide. Critical positions in country offices have been prioritized, supported by a substantial US$ 200 million funding allocation. Empowering WHO Representatives (WRs) with a revised delegation of authority has amplified their influence in management decisions. Furthermore, initiatives to enhance staff mobility and streamline communications across the WHO network have been swiftly implemented. Guided by the ARG, these decisive actions are propelling WHO's ongoing transformation efforts, accelerating our mission to drive impactful change where it's needed most—in countries.</p></div>
